rows.description: A child bites a lip, covers the mouth or looks down to hold back a giggle in a quiet moment. It shows awareness of rules and effort at self-control; a brief movement break or a whisper later helps release it.

rows.subtype: Laughing to fit in or mask [Regulating]
rows.description: A teenager laughs along with a group joke that feels unkind or hides hurt behind a laugh. Fake laughter can protect belonging but leave the person uneasy; choosing safe friends and a calm boundary such as that is not funny is healthier.

rows.subtype: Laughing in meetings and difficult talks [Regulating]
rows.description: A young professional uses a light laugh to ease tension, or holds one back in a solemn moment. A chuckle can build rapport, but laughing at a colleague's concern or a serious issue can seem dismissive.
A toddler who lacks words may grab, hit or bite when frustrated, tired or overwhelmed. It signals a strong feeling, not malice; adults can step in, name the feeling and show a safer action.
A preschooler says "You're mean!" or "It's your fault!" in a squabble. Blame is a simple way to explain distress; adults can help the child state what happened and what they wanted.

rows.subtype: Meeting the individual behind the label [Response]
rows.description: A teenager gets to know a person from a disliked group through shared work or sport. Cooperation toward a common goal is the strongest known way to soften group bias.
A mature adult checks their own assumptions, seeks out different views and speaks up when a group is mocked. They stay loyal to their own people without needing others to be lesser.

A parent who talks about periods, voice changes or body hair before they happen, in plain and unhurried words, gives a child confidence. Silence and giggling leave children to learn from rumour and fear.

A teenager learns that big feelings pass, and finds outlets such as sport, music, writing or talking to a trusted person. Waiting an hour before sending a message or slamming a door prevents many regrets.

rows.subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
rows.description: A child learns that getting help from a teacher or parent is not tattling but caring. They practise saying I need help and pointing at one specific adult.

rows.subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
rows.description: A teenager chooses a low-risk action such as checking on the victim, distracting the aggressor or calling an adult. Safe helping is a range of options, not a heroic all-or-nothing.

rows.subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
rows.description: An adult in an emergency points at one person and says you, call an ambulance, you, bring water. Naming someone breaks the diffusion of responsibility and gets action moving.

rows.subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
rows.description: A child who has enough at home feels sad on seeing a classmate's new bicycle and phone. The hurt comes from comparison, not from actual lack.

A teenager compares their marks, clothes or family situation with peers who are a step ahead, and feels cheated even though their own situation is decent. Feeling deprived depends on who one looks at.

A graduate who expected a job like their seniors got, and did not, feels bitter and entitled to something being withheld. Frustration is sharper when a group seems to be getting what they believed they deserved.
